Lewis acids and bases 
The acid-base concept can be extended beyond the Brensted-Lowry theory 
to include reactions that do not involve proton transfer. 
According to the Lewis theory, any species that accepts an electron pair is an 
acid while any species that donates an electron pair is a base. In the following 
reactions, ammonia acts as a Lewis base while the hydrogen cation and boron 
trifluoride act as Lewis acids:

The coordination bonds formed in these reactions (shown in red) are 
indistinguishable from “normal” covalent bonds, as they also involve shared 
electron pairs. Coordination bonds form in the same way as the bonds between 
nucleophiles and electrophiles in organic compounds. As follows from their 
definitions, all Lewis acids are electrophiles and all Lewis bases are nucleophiles. 
Example 21 
Suggest, with a reason, whether beryllium dihydride, methane and water 
can act as Lewis acids and/or Lewis bases. 
Solution 
BeH, is a Lewis acid because empty 2p orbitals in the beryllium atom can 
accept electron pairs. H,O is a Lewis base because the oxygen atom can 
donate its lone electron pairs to other species. The carbon atom in CH, has 
neither empty orbitals nor lone electron pairs, so methane cannot act as a 
Lewis acid or Lewis base. 
Coordination bonds are common in transition metal complexes, where the 
metal ion acts as a Lewis acid while ligands act as Lewis bases. For example, 
all agueous metal ions exist as agua complexes, in which oxygen atoms from

Nucleophilic substitution 
Nucleophilic substitution (S,) reactions involving halogenoalkanes and 
hydroxide ions were introduced in the SL section of this topic. 
Tertiary halogenoalkanes readily form tertiary carbocations, so they produce 
alcohols via a unimolecular two-step S 1 mechanism (figure 11). The first (slow) 
step of the reaction is the heterolytic breaking of the carbon-halogen bond 
that produces a carbocation. Tertiary carbocations are particularly stable 
because of the positive inductive effects of the three alkyl substituents. The 
second (fast) step involves the nucleophilic attack on the carbocation to 
produce the final reaction product, a tertiary alcohol.

The leaving group also affects the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution: 
S,1 reactions are favoured by large, weakly basic leaving groups, such as 
Br-and I, whereas SN2 reactions are more common for chloroalkanes. The 
fluoride ion, F-, is a very poor leaving group, so fluoroalkanes have very low 
reactivity, and their hydrolysis never follows the S, 1 pathway. 
The slow (rate-determining) step in SN1 reactions is the formation of the 
carbocation (figure 11). This step involves a single species, the halogenoalkane 
(RHal), so the reaction proceeds as a first-order process and is characterized 
by the rate equation v = k[RHal]. In contrast, the slow step in S_2 reactions 
involves two species, RHal and OH- (figure 12), so the reaction has an overall 
second order and is characterized by the rate equation v = k[RHal] [OH"]. The 
value of kand therefore the rate depend on the identity of the leaving group 
and nucleophile: large, weakly basic leaving groups and small, strongly basic, 
negatively charged nucleophiles generally increase the rates of S 2 reactions 
(table 13).

gives the main reaction product.

Experimental 
techniques Tool 1 
1.1 Addressing safety of self, others 
and the environment 
You should be able to: 
¢ recognize and address relevant safety, ethical and environmental issues in an investigation. 
Lab safety is an essential attribute of the learner profile. In conducting 
experimental work, you must take responsibility for your actions and their 
consequences. 
Accident prevention is the cornerstone of lab safety. It includes wearing 
personal protective equipment (PPE), conducting risk assessments, putting Nature of science 
the correct control measures in place and reducing risks by using safer alternatives. Accident prevention and waste 
prevention are two of the twelve 
Common PPE includes safety goggles, lab coats and protective gloves. principles of green chemistry. 
Certain experiments might require extra PPE, such as face shields, respirators 
and safety shoes. 
Before carrying out any experiment, a risk assessment must be completed. Risk 
assessments cover identification of hazards, ways of minimizing the risks and 
emergency measures that must be taken if something goes wrong. 
* Ahazard is a substance or activity that has the potential to cause 
harm (e.g. a toxic chemical or hot crucible). 
* Riskis the likelihood and severity of harm to the researcher, other lab 
users and the environment (e.g. poisoning by the toxic chemical or 
getting burned by the hot crucible). 
¢ A control measure is what must be done to minimize the risk 
(e.g. wear PPE, use tongs to pick up the hot crucible) and deal with 
accidents (e.g. have a first-aid kit and an emergency phone in the 
laboratory). 
Safety must be kept in mind before, during and after the experiment. To 
minimize the risks and protect the environment, the smallest possible 
quantities of chemicals must be used, and the waste must be disposed of in 
accordance with local rules and policies. When practical and safe, solvents 
and unreacted chemicals should be recovered and reused. The use of energy 
and water must also be minimized.

The formation of the complex ion, [NiCl4]2−(aq), can be represented as follows:
Ni2+(aq) + 4Cl−(aq) ⇌ [NiCl4]2−(aq)
In this reaction, Ni2+(aq) acts as a Lewis acid by accepting lone electron pairs from the ligands, Cl−(aq). In turn, the ligands act as Lewis bases by donating their lone electron pairs to the nickel(II) ion. Therefore, in terms of the Lewis theory, this reaction can be classified as a neutralization reaction.
See part (a). However, notice that the oxidation state of nickel(II) must be written as “+2”, not “2+”.
Butan-2-ol is the major product because its formation proceeds through the most stable (secondary) carbocation while the formation of butan-1-ol involves a less stable (primary) carbocation.
In the last step, the release of H+ can be facilitated by a molecule of water, as is shown in the solution to question 5(d) below.

Aromatic ring (six delocalized electrons that form a ring of high electron density above and below the plane of the six carbon atoms).
Nitric acid: the source of nitronium ions, +NO2, which act as electrophiles in reaction with benzene.
Sulfuric acid: the catalyst and dehydrating agent that facilitates the formation of nitronium ions and removes the reaction by-product (water) by converting it into hydronium ions, H3O+.
